extracted.intended_audience: criminal justices, judges, court lawyers, and criminalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judges and criminalists on evaluating the testimony, reliability, motives, and characteristic behavior of women (including old maids and hysterics) in criminal proceedings. Focuses on how feminine traits affect perception, judgment, honesty, and interrogative strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feminine conceit as indicator of sexuality and testimony reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: “By knowing the degree of feminine conceit we know also the vivacity of feminine sexuality... The use of them involves no possible error.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceit manifests in dress, love of tinsel and glitter, and quick display of new goods; it is criminologically important because showing off (e.g., immediately wearing newly acquired gauds) can betray ill-gotten gains. A criminalist who suspects theft may look first to a suspect’s wife or mistress because women often display fruits of crime. Examples: apprentices’ girlfriends getting new shawls; gypsy women trying on clothing while men complete a robbery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation for women's knowledge: conceit vs genuine interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Women often learn and accumulate information largely out of conceit – 'They learn only that it may be said of them, “They are scholars,” but for knowledge they care not at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a woman demonstrates knowledge, consider whether it serves to display status rather than arises from substantive interest. Conceit and curiosity are closely related; much female information-collection may be harmlessly explainable as display, but can also betray crimes or link to struggles for male attention. Interrogate motive when assessing the evidentiary value of learned facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old maid witness characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Old maids (childless, unmarried women of considerable age) commonly exhibit bitterness, envy, unpleasantness, hard judgment, difficulty forming new relationships, exaggerated fear, and prudery as simulation of innocence; as witnesses they 'always bring something new' and 'introduce a collection of doubts and suggestions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect an old maid’s testimony to introduce novel, suspicious, or personalizing interpretations of events; she may exaggerate personal threat or connect herself unnecessarily to matters. However, exceptions exist: some old maids are unusually kind, educated, and productive (founders of charities). Treat old-maid testimony cautiously, examine for bias stemming from loneliness, failed motherhood, or masculine traits, and investigate whether elements like 'intrigues, fanciful inheritances, and winnings in the lottery' point to an old maid’s involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hysteria: medico-legal significance and unreliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Hysterics have fixed ideas, attract attention, display persecutory hatred, and often produce elaborate unreasonable explanations; they may have 'diseased acuity' of senses (hearing and smell) and sometimes 'discover more than is there.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hysterical witnesses can generate false sensations and fixed false beliefs, and may feel or exhibit symptoms of imagined damages. The proper authority is the court physician; call medical experts whenever a hysteric is involved. Laymen lack specific symptoms to diagnose hysteria reliably; be aware that hysterics also often write anonymous letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feminine conception/intuitive perception (areas of reliability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Women 'conceive differently' and often have better conception in many contexts; in apprehension of situations, perception of attitudes, and 'tact' women can be 'superior, and more reliable individually, then ten men together.' Their process is rapid, unconscious intuition rather than reflective inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust women’s testimony where immediate perception, tact, or intuitive apprehension of personal environments is key. Their instinctive, unconscious conception can provide swifter and sometimes more certain impressions than drawn-out dialectical procedures. However, distinguish intuitive content from inferred conclusions when weighing reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of feminine inference and synthetic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Women tend to avoid inference and synthetic work; they 'let inference alone' and are less capable at reasoning that requires progressive composition or viewing distant/veiled matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about relying on female testimony in matters demanding extended inference, synthesis, or abstraction about distant consequences. Where inference is a factor, women’s statements may be less reliable; they may assert confidently without a logical foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity and personalizing tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity 'is another property that women lack. They tend always to think in personalities, and they conceive objects in terms of personal sympathies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a woman witness has personal relations or sympathies affecting perception. Before eliciting factual positions, identify her relations to parties (who are the people, ages, qualities). Allow brief general speech to discover her attitude; use that to adjust for personalization when interpreting her evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positiveness without grounds ('that must be')
rubrics_metrics.description: Women frequently assert 'that must be' when confused, desirous, or lacking reason; they may hide uncertainty under positivist language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a woman speaks with apparent positiveness, probe for the basis of her certainty. Beware that helping the witness with prompts ('of course you mean because') can elicit agreeable but unfounded confirmations. Distinguish genuine grounded assertions from reflexive 'that must be' statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to emotional extremes in judgment and crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Women are described as passionate and prone to extremes: 'women, committing crimes, go to extremes' and may plan complicated crimes that include purposeless deeds or act with immediate vengeful impulse then later remit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect polarized responses and extreme behavior in some female defendants or witnesses; consider that women may both overreact and then retract or change judgment when new information appears. Use this to interpret inconsistent or dramatic testimony and to hypothesize about motives or escalation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogation strategy: avoid quarrels and manage obstinacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal quarrels with women witnesses hurt the case; 'whoever quarrels with women is... in the condition of a man who must unceasingly polish lights.' Women have obstinacy that is not easily overcome by argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not engage in adversarial quarrels with most women witnesses; avoid trying to shame or browbeat them into concession. If seeking to correct a woman's misconception, prefer measured, non-confrontational methods, and know when to stop questioning. Momentary acquiescence to please a man is unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female attitudes toward money as motive indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Single women are characterized as either hoarders or wasters, displaying 'unintelligible arithmetic' about money; many women are uncurious about the source of a husband’s money despite knowing incomes and expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a woman’s pattern with money to infer motives: unreasonable demands or ignorance of source may precipitate theft, swindling, or other crimes by the husband to satisfy her. Investigate financial dynamics and consider women’s spending/hoarding habits when assessing motive for property crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuality and 'never quite ready' as explanatory factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Women have a notorious 'never quite ready' tendency, being typically ten minutes behind, which can explain failures in otherwise intelligent criminal plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider tardiness or failure to act at the right minute when reconstructing the chronology of criminal plans or missed opportunities. While not determinative, this trait can help explain why some plans failed or why certain defensive measures were ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism and attachment to objects as evidentiary clue
rubrics_metrics.description: Women show feminine conservatism: a stronger attachment to old things — ideas, jewelry, verses, proverbs — and are more likely to retain old letters and physical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When searching for physical evidence (old letters, tokens, implements of crime), prioritize female spaces/containers; women may retain incriminating items 'out of piety' or habit even after a man would have destroyed them. Use conservatism as a lead for locating corpora delicti.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty by omission versus active lying; handling through frankness
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction: 'Not to be honest, and to lie, are two different things.' Women more commonly practice dishonesty by suppression or indirectness ('Women always tell the truth, but not the whole truth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that female witnesses may omit or skirt truths due to social conditioning, shame, or prudery. Avoid indirect or prudish questioning that compels evasive answers; instead use simple, frank, open discussion to reduce compelled dishonesty. Do not assume physiological female propensity to lie more than men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological and behavioral tells when women lie
rubrics_metrics.description: Female offenders often betray themselves in 'the play of features, the eyes, the breast, the attitude' when lying; there is a feminine malaise visible in attempts to lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced observers may note nonverbal signs in women under deceptive statements, but be cautious: such cues are not definitive. Use them as supplementary indicators and corroborate with other evidence rather than as sole proof of deceit.
